Elements of Escape (Iti 72 2.5)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Elements of Escape (Iti 72 3.1)

“Knowing the escape from sensuality,
and form’s transcendence,
one always keen touches
the stilling of all activities.
Elements of Escape (Iti 72 4.1)

That mendicant sees rightly,
and when freed in regards to that,
that peaceful sage, with perfect insight,
has truly slipped their yoke.”
Elements of Escape (Iti 72 5.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
More Peaceful (Iti 73 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
More Peaceful (Iti 73 2.1)
“Mendicants, formless states are more peaceful than states of form; cessation is more peaceful than formless states.”
More Peaceful (Iti 73 2.2)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
More Peaceful (Iti 73 3.1)

“There are beings in the realm of luminous form,
and others stuck in the formless.
Not understanding cessation,
they return in future lives.
More Peaceful (Iti 73 4.1)

But the people who completely understand form,
not stuck in the formless,
released in cessation—
they are conquerors of death.
More Peaceful (Iti 73 5.1)

Having directly experienced the element free of death,
free of attachments;
having realized relinquishment
of attachments, the undefiled
fully awakened Buddha teaches
the sorrowless, stainless state.”
More Peaceful (Iti 73 6.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
A Child (Iti 74 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
A Child (Iti 74 2.1)
“These three kinds of children are found in the world. What three? One who betters their birth, one who equals their birth, one who fails their birth.
A Child (Iti 74 3.1)

And how does a child better their birth? It’s when a child’s parents have not gone for refuge to the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha. They kill living creatures, steal, commit sexual misconduct, lie, and consume intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor. They’re immoral, of bad character. But their child has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha. They don’t kill living creatures, steal, commit sexual misconduct, lie, or consume intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor. They’re ethical, of good character. That’s how a child betters their birth.
A Child (Iti 74 4.1)

And how does a child equal their birth? It’s when a child’s parents have gone for refuge to the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha. They don’t kill living creatures, steal, commit sexual misconduct, lie, or consume intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor. They’re ethical, of good character. And their child has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha. They don’t kill living creatures, steal, commit sexual misconduct, lie, or consume intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor. They’re ethical, of good character. That’s how a child equals their birth.
A Child (Iti 74 5.1)

And how does a child fail their birth? It’s when a child’s parents have gone for refuge to the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha. They don’t kill living creatures, steal, commit sexual misconduct, lie, or consume intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor. They’re ethical, of good character. But their child has not gone for refuge to the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha. They kill living creatures, steal, commit sexual misconduct, lie, and consume intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor. They’re immoral, of bad character. That’s how a child fails their birth. These are the three kinds of children found in the world.”
A Child (Iti 74 5.10)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
A Child (Iti 74 6.1)

“The astute wish for a child
who betters or equals their birth;
not one who fails their birth,
disgracing their family.
A Child (Iti 74 7.1)

These are the children in the world
who become lay devotees;
faithful, accomplished in ethics,
bountiful, rid of stinginess.
Like the moon freed from clouds,
they dazzle in the assemblies.”
A Child (Iti 74 8.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
A Rainless Cloud (Iti 75 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
A Rainless Cloud (Iti 75 2.1)
“Mendicants, these three individuals are found in the world. What three? One like a rainless cloud, one who rains locally, one who rains all over.
A Rainless Cloud (Iti 75 3.1)

And how is an individual like a rainless cloud? It’s when an individual doesn’t give to anyone at all—whether ascetics and brahmins, paupers, vagrants, supplicants, or beggars—such things as food, drink, clothing, vehicles; garlands, fragrance, and makeup; and bed, house, and lighting. That’s how an individual is like a rainless cloud.
A Rainless Cloud (Iti 75 4.1)

And how does an individual rain locally? It’s when an individual gives to some but not to others—whether ascetics and brahmins, paupers, vagrants, supplicants, or beggars—such things as food, drink, clothing, vehicles; garlands, fragrance, and makeup; and bed, house, and lighting. That’s how an individual rains locally.
A Rainless Cloud (Iti 75 5.1)

And how does an individual rain all over? It’s when an individual gives to everyone—whether ascetics and brahmins, paupers, vagrants, supplicants, or beggars—such things as food, drink, clothing, vehicles; garlands, fragrance, and makeup; and bed, house, and lighting. That’s how an individual rains all over. These are the three individuals found in the world.”
A Rainless Cloud (Iti 75 5.5)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
A Rainless Cloud (Iti 75 6.1)

“They don’t share the food and drink
they have acquired
with ascetics or brahmins,
with paupers, vagrants, or supplicants.
They’re like a rainless cloud,
they say, the meanest of men.
A Rainless Cloud (Iti 75 7.1)

They don’t give to some,
to some they provide.
They rain locally,
so say the wise.
A Rainless Cloud (Iti 75 8.1)

Compassionate for all beings,
that person distributes
abundant food upon request,
saying, ‘Give! Give!’
A Rainless Cloud (Iti 75 9.1)

The rain cloud rains forth,
having thundered and roared,
drenching the earth with water,
soaking the uplands and valleys.
A Rainless Cloud (Iti 75 10.1)

Even so, such an individual,
having accumulated wealth
by legitimate means,
through their own hard work,
rightly satisfies with food and drink
those who have become supplicants.”
A Rainless Cloud (Iti 75 11.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Wishing for Happiness (Iti 76 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Wishing for Happiness (Iti 76 2.1)

“Mendicants, an astute person who wishes for three kinds of happiness should take care of their ethics. What three? ‘May I be praised!’ ‘May I become rich!’ ‘When my body breaks up, after death, may I be reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm!’ An astute person who wishes for these three kinds of happiness should protect their precepts.”
Wishing for Happiness (Iti 76 2.5)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Wishing for Happiness (Iti 76 3.1)

“Wishing for three kinds of happiness—
praise, prosperity,
and to delight in heaven after passing away—
the wise would take care of their ethics.
Wishing for Happiness (Iti 76 4.1)

Though you do no wrong,
if you associate with one who does,
you’re suspected of wrong,
and your disrepute grows.
Wishing for Happiness (Iti 76 5.1)

Whatever kind of friend you make,
with whom you associate,
that’s how you become,
for so it is when you share your life.
Wishing for Happiness (Iti 76 6.1)

The one who associates and the one associated with,
the one contacted and the one who contacts another,
are like an arrow smeared with poison
that contaminates the quiver.
The attentive, fearing contamination,
would never have wicked comrades.
Wishing for Happiness (Iti 76 7.1)

A man who wraps
putrid fish in blades of grass
makes the grass stink—
so it is when associating with fools.
Wishing for Happiness (Iti 76 8.1)

But one who wraps
sandalwood incense in leaves
makes the leaves fragrant—
so it is when associating with the attentive.
Wishing for Happiness (Iti 76 9.1)

So, knowing they’ll end up
like the wrapping, the astute
would shun the wicked,
and befriend the good.
The wicked lead you to hell,
the good help you to a good place.”
Wishing for Happiness (Iti 76 10.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Fragile (Iti 77 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Fragile (Iti 77 2.1)
“This body is fragile, mendicants, consciousness is liable to fade away, and all attachments are impermanent, suffering, and perishable.”
Fragile (Iti 77 2.2)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Fragile (Iti 77 3.1)

“Knowing that the body is fragile,
that consciousness is faded,
and seeing the danger in attachments,
they go beyond birth and death.
Having attained ultimate peace,
evolved, they await their time.”
Fragile (Iti 77 4.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Converging Elements (Iti 78 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Converging Elements (Iti 78 2.1)

“Mendicants, sentient beings join together and converge because of an element: Those who have inferior convictions join together and converge with those who have inferior convictions. Those who have good convictions join together and converge with those who have good convictions.
Converging Elements (Iti 78 3.1)
In the past …
Converging Elements (Iti 78 4.1)
In the future …
Converging Elements (Iti 78 5.1)

At present, too, sentient beings join together and converge because of an element. Those who have inferior convictions join together and converge with those who have inferior convictions. Those who have good convictions join together and converge with those who have good convictions.”
Converging Elements (Iti 78 5.4)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Converging Elements (Iti 78 6.1)

“Socializing creates a snarl;
they’re cut off by being aloof.
If you’re lost in the middle of a great sea,
and you clamber up on a little log, you’ll sink.
Converging Elements (Iti 78 7.1)

So too, a person who lives well
sinks by relying on a lazy person.
Hence you should avoid such
a lazy person who lacks energy.
Converging Elements (Iti 78 8.1)

Dwell with the noble ones
who are secluded and determined
constantly energetic,
the astute who practice absorption.”
Converging Elements (Iti 78 9.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Decline (Iti 79 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Decline (Iti 79 2.1)
“These three things lead to the decline of a mendicant trainee. What three? It’s when a mendicant relishes work, talk, and sleep. These three things lead to the decline of a mendicant trainee.
Decline (Iti 79 3.1)

These three things don’t lead to the decline of a mendicant trainee. What three? It’s when a mendicant doesn’t relish work, talk, and sleep. These three things don’t lead to the decline of a mendicant trainee.”
Decline (Iti 79 3.7)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Decline (Iti 79 4.1)

“Restless, they relish
work, talk, and sleep.
Such a mendicant is incapable
of experiencing the highest awakening.
Decline (Iti 79 5.1)

That’s why one ought have few duties,
being wakeful not restless.
Such a mendicant is capable
of experiencing the highest awakening.”
Decline (Iti 79 6.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Thoughts (Iti 80 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Thoughts (Iti 80 2.1)

“Mendicants, there are these three unskillful thoughts. What three? The thought of status; of getting material things, honor, and popularity; and of fondness for others. These are the three unskillful thoughts.”
Thoughts (Iti 80 2.5)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Thoughts (Iti 80 3.1)

“One concerned with being looked up to,
with possessions, honor, and respect,
with sharing joys with friends,
is far from the ending of fetters.
Thoughts (Iti 80 4.1)

But one who gives up children and herds,
marriage and acquisitions—
such a mendicant is capable
of experiencing the highest awakening.”
Thoughts (Iti 80 5.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Esteem (Iti 81 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Esteem (Iti 81 2.1)

“I’ve seen, mendicants, sentient beings whose minds are overcome and overwhelmed by honor. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.
Esteem (Iti 81 3.1)
I’ve seen sentient beings whose minds are overcome and overwhelmed by not being honored. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.
Esteem (Iti 81 4.1)

I’ve seen sentient beings whose minds are overcome and overwhelmed by both honor and by not being honored. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.
Esteem (Iti 81 5.1)
Now, I don’t say this because I’ve heard it from some other ascetic or brahmin. I only say it because I’ve known, seen, and realized it for myself.”
Esteem (Iti 81 8.2)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Esteem (Iti 81 9.1)

“Whether they’re honored
or not honored, or both,
their immersion doesn’t waver
as they abide in the immeasurables.
Esteem (Iti 81 10.1)

They persistently practice absorption
with subtle view and discernment.
Rejoicing in the ending of grasping,
they’re said to be a true person.”
Esteem (Iti 81 11.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
The Cry of the Gods (Iti 82 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
The Cry of the Gods (Iti 82 2.1)

“Mendicants, these three cries are uttered among the gods on occasion. What three? When a noble disciple shaves off their hair and beard, dresses in ocher robes, and goes forth from the lay life to homelessness, the gods cry out: ‘This noble disciple intends to join battle with Māra!’ This is the first occasion a cry is uttered among the gods.
The Cry of the Gods (Iti 82 3.1)

Furthermore, when a noble disciple meditates pursuing the development of the seven qualities on the side of awakening, the gods cry out: ‘This noble disciple is joining battle with Māra!’ This is the second occasion a cry is uttered among the gods.
The Cry of the Gods (Iti 82 4.1)

Furthermore, when a noble disciple realizes the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements, the gods cry out: ‘This noble disciple has won victory in battle, establishing himself as foremost in battle!’ This is the third occasion a cry is uttered among the gods. These are the three cries that are uttered among the gods on occasion.”
The Cry of the Gods (Iti 82 4.5)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
The Cry of the Gods (Iti 82 5.1)

“Seeing the winner of the battle—
a disciple of the Buddha,
great of heart, intrepid—
even the deities revere them:
The Cry of the Gods (Iti 82 6.1)

‘Homage to you, O thoroughbred!
You won a battle hard to win!
Having defeated the army of death,
your liberation is unhindered.’
The Cry of the Gods (Iti 82 7.1)

And so the deities revere the one,
who has achieved their heart’s desire.
For they see nothing in them by means of which
they might fall under the sway of Death.”
The Cry of the Gods (Iti 82 8.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 2.1)

“Mendicants, when a god is due to pass away from the realm of the gods, five harbingers appear. Their flower-garlands wither; their clothes become soiled; they sweat from the armpits; their physical appearance deteriorates; and they no longer delight in their heavenly throne. When the other gods know that that godling is due to pass away, they wish them well in three ways: ‘Sir, may you go from here to a good place!
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 3.1)
When you have gone to a good place, may you be blessed with good fortune!
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 4.1)
When you have been blessed with good fortune, may you become well grounded!’”
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 5.1)
When he said this, one of the mendicants said to the Buddha, “Sir, what do the gods reckon to be going to a good place?
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 6.1)
What do they reckon to be blessed with good fortune?
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 7.1)
What do they reckon to become well grounded?”
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 8.1)
“It is human existence, mendicant, that the gods reckon to be going to a good place.
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 9.1)
When a human being gains faith in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One, that is what the gods reckon to be blessed with good fortune.
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 10.1)

When that faith in the Realized One is settled, rooted, and planted deep; when it’s strong and can’t be shifted by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world, that is what the gods reckon to become well grounded.”
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 11.1)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 12.1)

“When, with the fading of life,
a god passes from the realm of the gods,
the gods utter three cries
of well-wishing:
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 13.1)

‘Go, worthy sir, from here to a good place,
in the company of humans.
As a human being, gain supreme faith
in the true teaching.
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 14.1)

May that faith of yours be settled,
with roots planted deep,
unfaltering all life long
in the true teaching so well proclaimed.
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 15.1)

Having given up bad conduct
by way of body,
speech, and mind,
and whatever else is corrupt;
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 16.1)

and having done much good,
by way of body,
speech, and mind,
limitless, free of attachments;
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 17.1)

then, having made much worldly merit
by giving gifts,
establish other colleagues
in the true teaching, the spiritual life.’
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 18.1)

It is due to such sympathy
that when the gods know a god
is due to pass away, they wish them well:
‘Come back, god, again and again!’”
Five Harbingers (Iti 83 19.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
For the Welfare of the People (Iti 84 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
For the Welfare of the People (Iti 84 2.1)

“These three individuals, mendicants, arise in the world for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. What three? It’s when a Realized One arises in the world, perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed. He teaches Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. This is the first individual who arises in the world for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
For the Welfare of the People (Iti 84 3.1)

Furthermore, it’s when a mendicant is a perfected one, with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment. They teach Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And they reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. This is the second individual who arises in the world for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
For the Welfare of the People (Iti 84 4.1)

Furthermore, it’s when a disciple of that Teacher is a trainee, a learned practitioner with precepts and observances intact. They teach Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And they reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. This is the third individual who arises in the world for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. These are the three individuals who arise in the world for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.”
For the Welfare of the People (Iti 84 4.5)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
For the Welfare of the People (Iti 84 5.1)

“The Teacher is the first, the great seer,
following whom is the evolved disciple,
and then a trainee, a practitioner,
learned, with precepts and observances intact.
For the Welfare of the People (Iti 84 6.1)

These three are first among gods and humans,
beacons proclaiming the teaching!
They fling open the door to freedom from death,
freeing many from yokes.
For the Welfare of the People (Iti 84 7.1)

Following the path so well taught
by the unsurpassed caravan leader,
those who are diligent in the Holy One’s teaching
make an end of suffering in this very life.”
For the Welfare of the People (Iti 84 8.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Observing Ugliness (Iti 85 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Observing Ugliness (Iti 85 2.1)

“Mendicants, meditate observing the ugliness of the body. Let mindfulness of breathing be well-established internally on the present. Meditate observing the impermanence of all conditions. As you meditate observing the ugliness of the body, you will give up desire for the body. When mindfulness of breathing is well-established internally on the present, there will be no distressing external thoughts or wishes. When you meditate observing the impermanence of all conditions, ignorance is given up and knowledge arises.”
Observing Ugliness (Iti 85 2.7)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Observing Ugliness (Iti 85 3.1)

“Observing the ugliness of the body,
mindful of the breath,
one always keen sees
the stilling of all activities.
Observing Ugliness (Iti 85 4.1)

That mendicant sees rightly,
and when freed in regards to that,
that peaceful sage, with perfect insight,
has truly slipped their yoke.”
Observing Ugliness (Iti 85 5.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Practicing In Line With the Teaching (Iti 86 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Practicing In Line With the Teaching (Iti 86 2.1)

“Regarding a mendicant practicing in line with the teaching, it is in line with the teaching to declare that this is what it means to practice in line with the teaching. When speaking, they speak on the teaching, not against it. When thinking, they think on the teaching, not against it. And rejecting both, they meditate staying equanimous, mindful and aware.”
Practicing In Line With the Teaching (Iti 86 2.3)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Practicing In Line With the Teaching (Iti 86 3.1)

“Delighting in the teaching, enjoying the teaching,
contemplating the teaching,
a mendicant who recollects the teaching
doesn’t fall away from the true teaching.
Practicing In Line With the Teaching (Iti 86 4.1)

Whether walking or standing,
sitting or lying down,
with mind collected inside,
they attain only peace.”
Practicing In Line With the Teaching (Iti 86 5.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Destroyers of Sight (Iti 87 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Destroyers of Sight (Iti 87 2.1)

“Mendicants, these three unskillful thoughts are destroyers of sight, vision, and knowledge. They block wisdom, they’re on the side of distress, and they don’t lead to extinguishment. What three? Thoughts of sensuality, malice, and cruelty. These are the three unskillful thoughts that are destroyers of sight, vision, and knowledge. They block wisdom, they’re on the side of distress, and they don’t lead to extinguishment.
Destroyers of Sight (Iti 87 3.1)

These three skillful thoughts are creators of sight, vision, and knowledge. They grow wisdom, they’re on the side of solace, and they lead to extinguishment. What three? Thoughts of renunciation, good will, and harmlessness. These are the three skillful thoughts that are creators of sight, vision, and knowledge. They grow wisdom, they’re on the side of solace, and they lead to extinguishment.”
Destroyers of Sight (Iti 87 3.7)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Destroyers of Sight (Iti 87 4.1)

“Think the three skillful thoughts,
and get rid of the unskillful.
Quelling such thoughts and considerations,
like rain on the dust,
with a heart calmed of thought,
you’ll touch the state of peace right here.”
Destroyers of Sight (Iti 87 5.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Inner Stains (Iti 88 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Inner Stains (Iti 88 2.1)

“Mendicants, there are these three inner stains, inner foes, inner enemies, inner killers, and inner adversaries. What three? Greed, hate, and delusion. These three are inner stains, inner foes, inner enemies, inner killers, and inner adversaries.”
Inner Stains (Iti 88 2.7)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Inner Stains (Iti 88 3.1)

“Greed creates harm;
greed upsets the mind.
That person doesn’t recognize
the danger that arises within.
Inner Stains (Iti 88 4.1)

A greedy person doesn’t know the good.
A greedy person doesn’t see the truth.
When a person is beset by greed,
only blind darkness is left.
Inner Stains (Iti 88 5.1)

Those who have given up greed,
don’t get greedy even when provoked.
Greed falls off them
like a drop from a lotus-leaf.
Inner Stains (Iti 88 6.1)

Hate creates harm;
hate upsets the mind.
That person doesn’t recognize
the danger that arises within.
Inner Stains (Iti 88 7.1)

A hateful person doesn’t know the good.
A hateful person doesn’t see the truth.
When a person is beset by hate,
only blind darkness is left.
Inner Stains (Iti 88 8.1)

Those who have given up hate,
don’t get angry even when provoked.
Hate falls off them
like a ripe palmyra fruit from its stem.
Inner Stains (Iti 88 9.1)

Delusion creates harm;
delusion upsets the mind.
That person doesn’t recognize
the danger that arises within.
Inner Stains (Iti 88 10.1)

A deluded person doesn’t know the good.
A deluded person doesn’t see the truth.
When a person is beset by delusion,
only blind darkness is left.
Inner Stains (Iti 88 11.1)

Those who have given up delusion,
don’t get deluded even when provoked.
They banish all delusion,
as the rising sun the dark.”
Inner Stains (Iti 88 12.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
About Devadatta (Iti 89 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
About Devadatta (Iti 89 2.1)

“Mendicants, overcome and overwhelmed by three things that oppose the true teaching, Devadatta is going to a place of loss, to hell, there to remain for an eon, irredeemable. What three? Corrupt wishes … Bad friendship … When there is still more to be done, stopping half-way after achieving some trifling distinction. Overcome and overwhelmed by these three things that oppose the true teaching, Devadatta is going to a place of loss, to hell, there to remain for an eon, irredeemable.”
About Devadatta (Iti 89 2.7)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
About Devadatta (Iti 89 3.1)

“Let none of wicked desire
ever be reborn into this world.
And by this too you should know
the place where those of corrupt wishes go.
About Devadatta (Iti 89 4.1)

He once was considered astute,
deemed to be evolved,
his glory stood forth like a flame,
the renowned Devadatta.
About Devadatta (Iti 89 5.1)

Seduced by heedlessness,
he attacked the Realized One.
He has fallen to Avīci hell,
four-doored and terrifying.
About Devadatta (Iti 89 6.1)

When someone betrays the innocent,
who have done no wrong,
their bad deeds impact the one
with corrupt heart, lacking regard for others.
About Devadatta (Iti 89 7.1)

One might think to pollute
the ocean with a pot of poison,
but it wouldn’t work,
for the sea is terribly large.
About Devadatta (Iti 89 8.1)

So too when someone attacks
with words the Realized One—
rightly comported, of peaceful mind—
the words don’t take.
About Devadatta (Iti 89 9.1)

The astute would befriend one like this,
and follow them around.
A mendicant who walks the path
attains the ending of suffering.”
About Devadatta (Iti 89 10.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
The Best Kinds of Confidence (Iti 90 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
The Best Kinds of Confidence (Iti 90 2.1)

“Mendicants, these three kinds of confidence are the best. What three? Mendicants, the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, is said to be the best of all sentient beings—be they footless, with two feet, four feet, or many feet; with form or formless; with perception or without perception or with neither perception nor non-perception. Those who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the best. Having confidence in the best, the result is the best.
The Best Kinds of Confidence (Iti 90 3.1)

Fading away is said to be the best of all things whether conditioned or unconditioned. That is, the quelling of vanity, the removing of thirst, the uprooting of clinging, the breaking of the round, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, extinguishment. Those who have confidence in the teaching of fading away have confidence in the best. Having confidence in the best, the result is the best.
The Best Kinds of Confidence (Iti 90 4.1)

The Saṅgha of the Realized One’s disciples is said to be the best of all communities and groups. It consists of the four pairs, the eight individual persons. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world. Those who have confidence in the Saṅgha have confidence in the best. Having confidence in the best, the result is the best. These are the three best kinds of confidence.”
The Best Kinds of Confidence (Iti 90 4.5)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
The Best Kinds of Confidence (Iti 90 5.1)

“For those who, knowing the best teaching,
base their confidence on the best—
confident in the best Awakened One,
supremely worthy of a religious donation;
The Best Kinds of Confidence (Iti 90 6.1)

confident in the best teaching,
the bliss of fading and stilling;
confident in the best Saṅgha,
the supreme field of merit—
The Best Kinds of Confidence (Iti 90 7.1)

giving gifts to the best,
the best of merit grows:
the best lifespan, beauty,
fame, reputation, happiness, and strength.
The Best Kinds of Confidence (Iti 90 8.1)

An intelligent person gives to the best,
settled on the best teaching.
When they become a god or human,
they rejoice at reaching the best.”
The Best Kinds of Confidence (Iti 90 9.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Lifestyle (Iti 91 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Lifestyle (Iti 91 2.1)

“This is the last of lifestyles, mendicants, namely relying on alms. The world curses you: ‘You beggar, walking bowl in hand!’ Yet earnest gentlemen take it up for a good reason. Not to escape a summons by a king or a summons for a bandit, or because you were in debt or in fear, or in order to make a living. Rather, because they think: ‘I’m swamped by rebirth, old age, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I’m swamped by suffering, mired in suffering. Hopefully I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.’ That’s how this gentleman has gone forth. Yet they covet sensual pleasures; they’re infatuated, full of ill will and malicious intent. They are unmindful, lacking situational awareness and immersion, with straying minds and undisciplined faculties. Suppose there was a firebrand for lighting a funeral pyre, burning at both ends, and smeared with dung in the middle. It couldn’t be used as timber either in the village or the wilderness. I say that individual is just like this. They’ve missed out on the pleasures of the lay life, and haven’t fulfilled the goal of the ascetic life.”
Lifestyle (Iti 91 2.11)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Lifestyle (Iti 91 3.1)

“They’ve left behind the pleasures of the lay life,
and miss out on the goal of the ascetic life.
Ruining it, they throw it away,
and perish like a funeral firebrand.
Lifestyle (Iti 91 4.1)

Many who wear a scrap of ocher cloth
are unrestrained and wicked.
Being wicked, they are reborn in hell
due to their bad deeds.
Lifestyle (Iti 91 5.1)

It’d be better for the immoral and unrestrained
to eat an iron ball,
scorching, like a burning flame,
than to eat the nation’s alms.”
Lifestyle (Iti 91 6.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
The Corner of the Cloak (Iti 92 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
The Corner of the Cloak (Iti 92 2.1)

“Mendicants, suppose a mendicant were to hold the corner of my cloak and follow behind me step by step. Yet they covet sensual pleasures; they’re infatuated, full of ill will and malicious intent. They are unmindful, lacking situational awareness and immersion, with straying minds and undisciplined faculties. Then they are far from me, and I from them. Why is that? Because that mendicant does not see the teaching. Not seeing the teaching, they do not see me.
The Corner of the Cloak (Iti 92 3.1)

Suppose a mendicant were to live a hundred leagues away. Yet they do not covet sensual pleasures; they’re not infatuated, or full of ill will and malicious intent. They have established mindfulness, situational awareness and immersion, with unified mind and restrained faculties. Then they are close to me, and I to them. Why is that? Because that mendicant sees the teaching. Seeing the teaching, they see me.”
The Corner of the Cloak (Iti 92 3.7)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
The Corner of the Cloak (Iti 92 4.1)

“One full of desire and distress
may follow close behind,
yet see how distant they are—
the stirred from the still,
the burning from the quenched,
the greedy from the greedless.
The Corner of the Cloak (Iti 92 5.1)

An astute person who has understood
and directly known the teaching,
grows calm, as unperturbed
as a lake free of wind.
The Corner of the Cloak (Iti 92 6.1)

See how close they are—
the still to the still,
the quenched to the quenched,
the greedless to the greedless.”
The Corner of the Cloak (Iti 92 7.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Fire (Iti 93 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Fire (Iti 93 2.1)
“Mendicants, there are these three fires. What three? The fires of greed, hate, and delusion. These are the three fires.”
Fire (Iti 93 2.5)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Fire (Iti 93 3.1)
Fire (Iti 93 4.1)

and, bewildered by the fire of delusion,
they miss the teaching of the noble ones.
Not recognizing these three fires,
people are caught up in substantial reality.
Fire (Iti 93 5.1)

They fill the ranks of hell,
of birth as an animal,
or of titans and ghosts,
not freed from Māra’s bonds.
Fire (Iti 93 6.1)

But as to those committed day and night
to the teaching of the Buddha:
they extinguish the fire of greed,
always perceiving ugliness;
Fire (Iti 93 7.1)

while those supreme men
extinguish the fire of hate with love;
and the fire of delusion with the wisdom
that leads to penetration.
Fire (Iti 93 8.1)

Having extinguished these fires, alert,
tireless all day and night,
they become fully extinguished,
completely transcending suffering.
Fire (Iti 93 9.1)

Seers of the noble truths, knowledge masters,
the astute, understanding rightly,
directly know the ending of rebirth,
they come not back to future lives.”
Fire (Iti 93 10.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Examination (Iti 94 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Examination (Iti 94 2.1)

“A mendicant should examine in whatever way such that, while examining, consciousness would neither be scattered nor diffused externally, nor stuck internally, and they would not be anxious because of grasping. When consciousness is neither scattered nor diffused externally, nor stuck internally, and they are not anxious because of grasping, there is no coming to be of the origin of suffering—of rebirth, old age, and death in the future.”
Examination (Iti 94 2.3)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Examination (Iti 94 3.1)

“For one who has given up seven chains,
a mendicant who has cut the cord,
transmigration through births is finished,
there’ll be no more future lives for them.”
Examination (Iti 94 4.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Provided With Pleasure (Iti 95 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Provided With Pleasure (Iti 95 2.1)

“Mendicants, there are these three ways of being provided with sensual pleasures. What three? Some sensual pleasures are simply present; some are for those who love to create; and some are for those who control what is created by others. These are the three ways of being provided with sensual pleasures.”
Provided With Pleasure (Iti 95 2.5)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Provided With Pleasure (Iti 95 3.1)

“Sensual pleasures that are simply present,
gods who control what is created by others,
gods who love to create,
and others who indulge in sensual pleasures—
They go from this state to another,
but don’t escape transmigration.
Provided With Pleasure (Iti 95 4.1)

Knowing this danger
in sensual indulgence, an astute person
would forsake all sensual pleasures,
both human and heavenly.
Provided With Pleasure (Iti 95 5.1)

Having cut the stream so hard to pass,
that’s tied to pleasant seeming things,
they become fully extinguished,
completely transcending suffering.
Provided With Pleasure (Iti 95 6.1)

Seers of the noble truths, knowledge masters,
the astute, understanding rightly,
directly know the ending of rebirth,
they come not back to future lives.”
Provided With Pleasure (Iti 95 7.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Yoked to Sensual Pleasures (Iti 96 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Yoked to Sensual Pleasures (Iti 96 2.1)

“Mendicants, one yoked to both sensual pleasures and rebirth is a returner, who comes back to this place. One unyoked from sensual pleasures but still yoked to rebirth is a non-returner, who comes not back to this place. One unyoked from both sensual pleasures and rebirth is a perfected one, who has ended defilements.”
Yoked to Sensual Pleasures (Iti 96 2.4)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Yoked to Sensual Pleasures (Iti 96 3.1)

“Yoked to both sensual pleasures
and the desire to be reborn in a future life;
sentient beings continue to transmigrate,
with ongoing birth and death.
Yoked to Sensual Pleasures (Iti 96 4.1)

Those who’ve given up sensual pleasures
without attaining the end of defilements,
and are still yoked to being reborn,
are said to be non-returners.
Yoked to Sensual Pleasures (Iti 96 5.1)

Those who have cut off doubt,
and ended conceit and future lives,
they’re the ones in this world who’ve truly crossed over,
having reached the ending of defilements.”
Yoked to Sensual Pleasures (Iti 96 6.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Good Morals (Iti 97 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Good Morals (Iti 97 2.1)
“Mendicants, in this teaching and training a mendicant of good morals, good practice, and good wisdom is called consummate, accomplished, a supreme person.
Good Morals (Iti 97 3.1)

And how does a mendicant have good morals? It’s when a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they’ve undertaken. That’s how a mendicant has good morals. Such is one of good morality.
Good Morals (Iti 97 4.1)

And how does one have good practice? It’s when a mendicant meditates pursuing the development of the seven qualities on the side of awakening. That’s how a mendicant has good practice. Such is one of good morality and good practice.
Good Morals (Iti 97 5.1)

And how does one have good wisdom? It’s when a mendicant realizes the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements. That’s how a mendicant has good wisdom;
Good Morals (Iti 97 6.1)
Such is one of good morals, good practice, and good wisdom, who in this teaching and training is called consummate, accomplished, a supreme person.”
Good Morals (Iti 97 6.2)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Good Morals (Iti 97 7.1)

“Who does nothing wrong
by body, speech or mind,
is said to be one of good morals,
a conscientious mendicant.
Good Morals (Iti 97 8.1)

Who has well developed the seven
factors that lead to awakening
is said to be one good practice,
an unpretentious mendicant.
Good Morals (Iti 97 9.1)

Who understands for themselves
the end of suffering in this life
is said to be one good wisdom,
an undefiled mendicant.
Good Morals (Iti 97 10.1)

One accomplished in these three things,
untroubled, with doubts cut off,
unattached to anything in the world,
has given up everything, they say.”
Good Morals (Iti 97 11.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Giving (Iti 98 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Giving (Iti 98 2.1)
“There are, mendicants, these two gifts. A gift of things of the flesh and a gift of the teaching. The better of these two gifts is the gift of the teaching.
Giving (Iti 98 3.1)
There are these two kinds of sharing. Sharing things of the flesh and sharing the teaching. The better of these two kinds of sharing is sharing the teaching.
Giving (Iti 98 4.1)
There are these two kinds of support. Support in things of the flesh and support in the teaching. The better of these two kinds of support is support in the teaching.”
Giving (Iti 98 4.4)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Giving (Iti 98 5.1)

“It is said to be the supreme, ultimate gift,
and the sharing praised by the Buddha;
what wise and sensible person, confident in the best of fields,
would not sow a such timely gift?
Giving (Iti 98 6.1)

For those who are diligent in the dispensation of the Holy One,
both those who speak and those who listen,
confident in the dispensation of the Holy One,
such a gift purifies the highest goal.”
Giving (Iti 98 7.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
The Three Knowledges (Iti 99 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
The Three Knowledges (Iti 99 2.1)
“Mendicants, I define a brahmin in terms of the teaching as one who is master of the three knowledges, not the other who merely repeats what they are told.
The Three Knowledges (Iti 99 3.1)

How so? It’s when a mendicant recollects many kinds of past lives. That is: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand rebirths; many eons of the world contracting, many eons of the world expanding, many eons of the world contracting and expanding. They remember: ‘There, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn somewhere else. There, too, I was named this, my clan was that, I looked like this, and that was my food. This was how I felt pleasure and pain, and that was how my life ended. When I passed away from that place I was reborn here.’ And so they recollect their many kinds of past lives, with features and details. This is the first knowledge they achieved. Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.
The Three Knowledges (Iti 99 4.1)

Furthermore, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, a mendicant sees sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds: ‘These dear beings did bad things by way of body, speech, and mind. They denounced the noble ones; they had wrong view; and they chose to act out of that wrong view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. These dear beings, however, did good things by way of body, speech, and mind. They never denounced the noble ones; they had right view; and they chose to act out of that right view. When their body broke up, after death, they were reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ And so, with clairvoyance that is purified and superhuman, they see sentient beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in a good place or a bad place. They understand how sentient beings pass on according to their deeds. This is the second knowledge they achieved. Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.
The Three Knowledges (Iti 99 5.1)

Furthermore, a mendicant realizes the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom. And they live having realized it with their own insight in this very life due to the ending of defilements. This is the third knowledge which they achieved. Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute. That’s how I define a brahmin in terms of the teaching as one who is master of the three knowledges, not the other who merely repeats what they are told.”
The Three Knowledges (Iti 99 5.4)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
The Three Knowledges (Iti 99 6.1)

“One who knows their past lives,
sees heaven and places of loss,
and has attained the end of rebirth,
is a sage of perfect insight.
The Three Knowledges (Iti 99 7.1)

Because of these three knowledges
a brahmin is a master of the three knowledges.
That’s who I call a three-knowledge master,
and not the other who repeats what they are told.”
The Three Knowledges (Iti 99 8.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
The Brahmin’s Offering of the Teaching (Iti 100 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
The Brahmin’s Offering of the Teaching (Iti 100 2.1)

“I, mendicants, am a brahmin, committed to charity, always open-handed, bearing my final body, a healer, a surgeon. You are my bosom sons, born from my mouth, born of the teaching, created by the teaching, heirs in the teaching, not in things of the flesh.
The Brahmin’s Offering of the Teaching (Iti 100 3.1)
There are these two gifts. A gift of things of the flesh and a gift of the teaching. The better of these two gifts is the gift of the teaching.
The Brahmin’s Offering of the Teaching (Iti 100 4.1)
There are these two kinds of sharing. Sharing things of the flesh and sharing the teaching. The better of these two kinds of sharing is sharing the teaching.
The Brahmin’s Offering of the Teaching (Iti 100 5.1)
There are these two kinds of support. Support in things of the flesh and support in the teaching. The better of these two kinds of support is support in the teaching.
The Brahmin’s Offering of the Teaching (Iti 100 6.1)
There are these two offerings. An offering of things of the flesh and an offering of the teaching. The better of these two offerings is an offering of the teaching.”
The Brahmin’s Offering of the Teaching (Iti 100 6.4)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
The Brahmin’s Offering of the Teaching (Iti 100 7.1)

“The Realized One, compassionate for all living creatures,
unstintingly offers teaching.
Sentient beings revere him, first among gods and humans,
who has gone beyond rebirth.”
The Brahmin’s Offering of the Teaching (Iti 100 8.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Easy to Find (Iti 101 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Easy to Find (Iti 101 2.1)

“Mendicants, these four trifles are easy to find and are blameless. What four? Rag-robes … A lump of almsfood … Lodgings at the root of a tree … Rancid urine as medicine … These four trifles are easy to find and are blameless. When a mendicant is content with trifles that are easy to find, they have one of the factors of the ascetic life, I say.”
Easy to Find (Iti 101 2.9)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Easy to Find (Iti 101 3.1)

“When one is content with what’s blameless,
trifling, and easy to find,
they don’t get distressed
about lodgings, robes,
food, and drink,
and they’re not obstructed anywhere.
Easy to Find (Iti 101 4.1)

These qualities are said to be
integral to the ascetic life.
They’re mastered by a mendicant,
content and diligent.”
Easy to Find (Iti 101 5.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
The Ending of Defilements (Iti 102 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
The Ending of Defilements (Iti 102 2.1)

“Mendicants, I say that the ending of defilements is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know or see. For one who knows and sees what? The ending of defilements is for one who knows and sees suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. The ending of the defilements is for one who knows and sees this.”
The Ending of Defilements (Iti 102 2.5)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
The Ending of Defilements (Iti 102 3.1)

“As a trainee trains,
following the straight road,
first they know about ending;
enlightenment follows in the same lifetime.
The Ending of Defilements (Iti 102 4.1)

Then to one freed through enlightenment
the knowledge of ending arises,
the supreme knowledge of freedom,
with the ending of the fetters.
The Ending of Defilements (Iti 102 5.1)

Not by the lazy,
or by fools who don’t understand
may this be realized—extinguishment,
the release from all ties.”
The Ending of Defilements (Iti 102 6.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Ascetics and Brahmins (Iti 103 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Ascetics and Brahmins (Iti 103 2.1)

“Mendicants, there are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. I don’t deem them as true ascetics and brahmins. Those venerables don’t realize the goal of life as an ascetic or brahmin, and don’t live having realized it with their own insight in this very life.
Ascetics and Brahmins (Iti 103 3.1)

There are ascetics and brahmins who truly understand about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. I regard them as true ascetics and brahmins. Those venerables realize the goal of life as an ascetic or brahmin, and live having realized it with their own insight.”
Ascetics and Brahmins (Iti 103 3.3)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Ascetics and Brahmins (Iti 103 4.1)

“There are those who don’t understand suffering
and suffering’s cause,
and where all suffering
cease with no residue left behind.
And they do not know the path
that leads to the stilling of suffering.
Ascetics and Brahmins (Iti 103 5.1)

They lack the heart’s release,
as well as the release by wisdom.
Unable to make an end,
they continue to be reborn and grow old.
Ascetics and Brahmins (Iti 103 6.1)

But there are those who understand suffering
and suffering’s cause,
and where all suffering
cease with no residue left behind.
And they understand the path
that leads to the stilling of suffering.
Ascetics and Brahmins (Iti 103 7.1)

They’re endowed with the heart’s release,
as well as the release by wisdom.
Able to make an end,
they don’t continue to be reborn and grow old.”
Ascetics and Brahmins (Iti 103 8.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Accomplished in Ethics (Iti 104 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Accomplished in Ethics (Iti 104 2.1)

“Mendicants, take a mendicant who is accomplished in ethics, immersion, wisdom, freedom, and the knowledge and vision of freedom. They advise and instruct. They educate, encourage, fire up, and inspire, and can rightly explain the true teaching. Even the sight of those mendicants is very helpful, I say. Even to hear them, approach them, pay homage to them, recollect them, or go forth after them is very helpful, I say. Why is that? For one who frequents and associates with such mendicants, their incomplete spectrum of ethics is completed. Their incomplete spectrum of immersion … wisdom … freedom … knowledge and vision of freedom is completed. Such mendicants are called ‘teachers’, ‘caravan leaders’, ‘strife-discarders’, ‘dispellers of darkness’, ‘bringers of light’, ‘luminaries’, ‘lamps’, ‘candlebearers’, ‘beacons’, ‘noble ones’, and ‘clear-eyed ones’.”
Accomplished in Ethics (Iti 104 2.10)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Accomplished in Ethics (Iti 104 3.1)

“This is a reason for joy
for those who understand:
that is, those who are evolved,
the noble ones living righteously.
Accomplished in Ethics (Iti 104 4.1)

They illuminate the true teaching,
beacons beaming light,
the attentive ones bringing light,
clear-eyed ones with strife discarded.
Accomplished in Ethics (Iti 104 5.1)

Having heard their instruction,
the astute, understanding rightly,
directly know the ending of rebirth,
they come not back to future lives.”
Accomplished in Ethics (Iti 104 6.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
The Arising of Craving (Iti 105 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
The Arising of Craving (Iti 105 2.1)

“Mendicants, there are four things that give rise to craving in a mendicant. What four? For the sake of robes, almsfood, lodgings, or rebirth in this or that state. These are the four things that give rise to craving in a mendicant.”
The Arising of Craving (Iti 105 2.8)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
The Arising of Craving (Iti 105 3.1)

“Craving is a person’s partner
as they transmigrate on this long journey.
They go from this state to another,
but don’t escape transmigration.
The Arising of Craving (Iti 105 4.1)

Knowing this danger,
that craving is the cause of suffering—
rid of craving, free of grasping,
a mendicant would wander mindful.”
The Arising of Craving (Iti 105 5.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
With Divinity (Iti 106 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
With Divinity (Iti 106 2.1)

“Mendicants, a family where the children honor their parents in their home is said to live with Divinity. A family where the children honor their parents in their home is said to live with the elder gods. A family where the children honor their parents in their home is said to live with the first tutors. A family where the children honor their parents in their home is said to live with those worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods.
With Divinity (Iti 106 3.1)

‘Divinity’ is a term for your parents. ‘Elder gods’ is a term for your parents. ‘First tutors’ is a term for your parents. ‘Worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods’ is a term for your parents. Why is that? Parents are very helpful to their children, they raise them, nurture them, and show them the world.”
With Divinity (Iti 106 3.7)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
With Divinity (Iti 106 4.1)

“Parents are said to be ‘Divinity’
and ‘first tutors’.
They’re worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods from their children,
for they love their offspring.
With Divinity (Iti 106 5.1)

Therefore an astute person
would revere them and honor them
with food and drink,
clothes and bedding,
anointing and bathing,
and by washing their feet.
With Divinity (Iti 106 6.1)

Because they serve
their parents like this,
they’re praised in this life by the astute,
and they depart to rejoice in heaven.”
With Divinity (Iti 106 7.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Very Helpful (Iti 107 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Very Helpful (Iti 107 2.1)

“Mendicants, brahmins and householders are very helpful to you, as they provide you with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick. And you are very helpful to brahmins and householders, as you teach them the Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And you reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. That is how this spiritual path is lived supporting each other in order to cross over the flood and make a complete end of suffering.”
Very Helpful (Iti 107 2.4)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Very Helpful (Iti 107 3.1)

“The home-dweller and the homeless,
supporting each other,
find success in the true teaching,
the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.
Very Helpful (Iti 107 4.1)

The homeless receive requisites
from the home-dwellers:
robes and lodgings
to shelter from harsh conditions.
Very Helpful (Iti 107 5.1)

Relying on the Holy One,
layfolk and householders of discernment
place faith in the perfected ones,
meditators of noble wisdom.
Very Helpful (Iti 107 6.1)

Having practiced the teaching here,
the path that goes to a good place,
they delight in the heavenly realm,
enjoying all the pleasures they desire.”
Very Helpful (Iti 107 7.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Deceivers (Iti 108 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Deceivers (Iti 108 2.1)

“Mendicants, those mendicants who are deceivers and flatterers, pompous and fake, insolent and scattered: those mendicants are no followers of mine. They’ve left this teaching and training, and they don’t achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training. But those mendicants who are genuine, not flatterers, attentive, amenable, and serene: those mendicants are followers of mine. They haven’t left this teaching and training, and they achieve growth, improvement, or maturity in this teaching and training.”
Deceivers (Iti 108 2.5)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Deceivers (Iti 108 3.1)

“Those who are deceivers and flatterers, pompous and fake,
insolent and scattered:
these don’t grow in the teaching
that was taught by the perfected Buddha.
Deceivers (Iti 108 4.1)

But those who are genuine, not flatterers, attentive,
amenable, and serene:
these do grow in the teaching
that was taught by the perfected Buddha.”
Deceivers (Iti 108 5.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
A River (Iti 109 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
A River (Iti 109 2.1)

“Suppose a person was being carried along by a river current that seemed nice and pleasant. If a person with clear eyes saw them, they’d say: ‘My man, even though the river current carrying you along seems nice and pleasant, downstream there is a lake with waves and whirlpools, saltwater crocodiles and monsters. When you reach there it will result in death or deadly pain.’ Then, when they heard what was said, they’d paddle against the stream using their hands and feet.
A River (Iti 109 3.1)
I’ve made up this simile to make a point. And this is the point. ‘River current’ is a term for craving.
A River (Iti 109 4.1)
‘Seeming nice and pleasant’ is a term for the six interior sense fields.
A River (Iti 109 5.1)
‘A downstream lake’ is a term for the five lower fetters.
A River (Iti 109 6.1)
‘Danger of waves’ is a term for anger and distress.
A River (Iti 109 7.1)
‘Whirlpool’ is a term for the five kinds of sensual stimulation.
A River (Iti 109 8.1)
‘Saltwater crocodiles and monsters’ is a term for ladies.
A River (Iti 109 9.1)
‘Against the stream’ is a term for renunciation.
A River (Iti 109 10.1)
‘Paddling with hands and feet’ is a term for rousing energy.
A River (Iti 109 11.1)
‘A person with clear eyes’ is a term for the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha.”
A River (Iti 109 11.2)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
A River (Iti 109 12.1)

“In pain they’d give up sensual pleasures,
aspiring to the future sanctuary from the yoke.
With deep understanding and heart well freed,
they’d experience universal liberation.
That knowledge master who has completed the spiritual journey,
and gone to the end of the world, is called ‘one who has gone beyond’.”
A River (Iti 109 13.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Walking (Iti 110 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Walking (Iti 110 2.1)

“Mendicants, suppose a mendicant has a sensual, malicious, or cruel thought while walking. They tolerate it and don’t give it up, dispel it, eliminate it, and obliterate it. Such a mendicant is said to be ‘not keen or prudent, always lazy, and lacking energy’ when walking.
Walking (Iti 110 3.1)

Suppose a mendicant has a sensual, malicious, or cruel thought while standing … sitting … or when lying down while awake. They tolerate it and don’t give it up, dispel it, eliminate it, and obliterate it. Such a mendicant is said to be ‘not keen or prudent, always lazy, and lacking energy’ when lying down while awake.
Walking (Iti 110 6.1)

Suppose a mendicant has a sensual, malicious, or cruel thought while walking. They don’t tolerate them, but give them up, dispel them, eliminate them, and obliterate them. Such a mendicant is said to be ‘keen and prudent, always energetic and resolute’ when walking.
Walking (Iti 110 7.1)

Suppose a mendicant has a sensual, malicious, or cruel thought while standing … sitting … or when lying down while awake. They don’t tolerate it, but give it up, dispel it, eliminate it, and obliterate it. Such a mendicant is said to be ‘keen and prudent, always energetic and resolute’ when lying down while awake.”
Walking (Iti 110 9.4)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Walking (Iti 110 10.1)

“Whether walking or standing,
sitting or lying down,
one who thinks a bad thought
to do with the domestic life
Walking (Iti 110 11.1)

is practicing the wrong way,
lost among things that delude;
such a mendicant is incapable
of experiencing the highest awakening.
Walking (Iti 110 12.1)

But one who, whether standing or walking,
sitting or lying down,
has calmed their thoughts,
loving peace of mind;
such a mendicant is capable
of experiencing the highest awakening.”
Walking (Iti 110 13.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
Accomplishment in Ethics (Iti 111 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
Accomplishment in Ethics (Iti 111 2.1)

“Mendicants, live by the ethical precepts and the monastic code. Live restrained in the monastic code, conducting yourselves well and resorting for alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, keep the rules you’ve undertaken.
Accomplishment in Ethics (Iti 111 3.1)
When you’ve done this, what more is there to do?
Accomplishment in Ethics (Iti 111 4.1)

Suppose a mendicant has got rid of desire and ill will while walking, and has given up dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. Their energy is roused up and unflagging, their mindfulness is established and lucid, their body is tranquil and undisturbed, and their mind is immersed and unified in samādhi. Such a mendicant is said to be ‘keen and prudent, always energetic and resolute’ when walking.
Accomplishment in Ethics (Iti 111 5.1)
Suppose a mendicant has got rid of desire and ill will while standing …
Accomplishment in Ethics (Iti 111 6.1)
sitting …
Accomplishment in Ethics (Iti 111 7.1)
or when lying down while awake. Such a mendicant is said to be ‘keen and prudent, always energetic and resolute’ when lying down while awake.”
Accomplishment in Ethics (Iti 111 7.3)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
Accomplishment in Ethics (Iti 111 8.1)

“Carefully walking, carefully standing,
carefully sitting, carefully lying;
a mendicant carefully bends their limbs,
and carefully extends them.
Accomplishment in Ethics (Iti 111 9.1)

Above, below, all round,
as far as the planet extends;
they scrutinize the rise and fall
of phenomena such as the aggregates.
Accomplishment in Ethics (Iti 111 10.1)

Meditating diligently like this,
peaceful, not restless,
training in what leads to serenity of heart,
always staying mindful;
they call that sort of mendicant
‘always determined’.”
Accomplishment in Ethics (Iti 111 11.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
The World (Iti 112 1.1)
This was said by the Buddha, the Perfected One: that is what I heard.
The World (Iti 112 2.1)

“Mendicants, the world has been understood by the Realized One; and he is detached from the world. The origin of the world has been understood by the Realized One; and he has given up the origin of the world. The cessation of the world has been understood by the Realized One; and he has realized the cessation of the world. The practice that leads to the cessation of the world has been understood by the Realized One; and he has developed the practice that leads to the cessation of the world.
The World (Iti 112 3.1)

In this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—whatever is seen, heard, thought, known, attained, sought, and explored by the mind, all that has been understood by the Realized One. That’s why he’s called the ‘Realized One’.
The World (Iti 112 4.1)

From the night when the Realized One awakens to the supreme perfect awakening until the night he becomes fully extinguished—in the element of extinguishment with no residue—everything he speaks, says, and expresses is real, not otherwise. That’s why he’s called the ‘Realized One’.
The World (Iti 112 5.1)
The Realized One does as he says, and says as he does. Since this is so, that’s why he’s called the ‘Realized One’.
The World (Iti 112 6.1)

In this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—the Realized One is the vanquisher, the unvanquished, the universal seer, the wielder of power. That’s why he’s called the ‘Realized One’.”
The World (Iti 112 6.3)
The Buddha spoke this matter. On this it is said:
The World (Iti 112 7.1)

“Directly knowing the whole world as it is,
and everything in it,
he is detached from the whole world,
uninvolved with the whole world.
The World (Iti 112 8.1)

That attentive one is the vanquisher of all
who is released from all ties.
He has reached ultimate peace:
extinguishment, fearing nothing from any quarter.
The World (Iti 112 9.1)

He is the Buddha, with defilements ended,
untroubled, with doubts cut off.
He has attained the end of all deeds,
freed with the ending of attachments.
The World (Iti 112 10.1)

That Blessed One is the Buddha,
he is the supreme lion,
in all the world with its gods,
he turns the divine wheel.
The World (Iti 112 11.1)

And so those gods and humans,
who have gone to the Buddha for refuge,
come together and revere him,
even the deities revere him:
The World (Iti 112 12.1)

‘Tamed, he is the best of tamers,
peaceful, he is the seer among the peaceful,
liberated, he is the foremost of liberators,
crossed over, he is the most excellent of guides across.’
The World (Iti 112 13.1)

And so they revere him,
great of heart and intrepid.
In the world with its gods,
he has no rival.”
The World (Iti 112 14.1)
This too is a matter that was spoken by the Blessed One: that is what I heard.
The World (Iti 112 17.5)
The So it Was Said is finished.
Sure Bet: a past life story (Ja 1 1.1)
Homage to him, the blessed one, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!
Sure Bet: a past life story (Ja 1 2.1)

Some stand on a sure bet,
while sophists speak of a second way.
An intelligent person, knowing this,
would take up the sure bet.
Sandy Waste: a past life story (Ja 2 1.1)

Digging untiringly in a sandy waste,
there at the underground stream he found water.
In the same way, a sage with strength aroused
untiringly finds the peace of the heart.
The Wanton Merchant: a past life story (Ja 3 1.1)

If you fail to achieve
certainty regarding the true teaching
you’ll regret it for a long time,
like this wanton merchant.
The Little Financier: a past life story (Ja 4 1.1)

Even with a little capital
the intelligent and clear-seeing man
uplifts himself,
like a tiny flame when fanned.
A Cup of Rice: a past life story (Ja 5 1.1)

“Speak, O King: what value has a cup of rice
for the pricing of horses?”
“He values a cup of rice
at Varanasi with its suburbs!”
Godly Qualities: a past life story (Ja 6 1.1)

Endowed with conscience and prudence,
and comprised of bright qualities,
the good and true persons in the world
are said to have godly qualities.
The Wood Gatherer: a past life story (Ja 7 1.1)

I am your son, Great King!
Provide for me, ruler of the people.
The king provides for others,
what then of his own offspring?
The Chief: a past life story (Ja 8 1.1)

Even though they do not hurry,
one who hopes for the fruit succeeds.
I am one whose spiritual life has ripened:
know this, chief.
Maghadeva: a past life story (Ja 9 1.1)

Growing on top of my head,
these thieves of life have sprouted.
Messengers of the gods have appeared—
it is time for me to go forth.
Living at Ease: a past life story (Ja 10 1.1)

He who is not guarded by others,
and who does not guard others,
truly sleeps at ease, O King,
unconcerned for sensual pleasures.
The Deer Named Lucky Spot: a past life story (Ja 11 1.1)

The virtuous ones prosper,
who live extending protection.
See Lucky Spot coming,
surrounded by their family circle;
then see this Black Mark,
bereft of family.
The Deer Named Banyan: a past life story (Ja 12 1.1)

Befriend only Banyan,
stay away from Branch.
Better is death with Banyan
than life with Branch.
The Arrow: a past life story (Ja 13 1.1)

Curse the dart, the arrow
that deeply strikes a man.
Curse the nation
where women rule.
Those creatures are cursed
who fall to women’s sway.
The Wind-deer: a past life story (Ja 14 1.1)

Nothing, it seems, is worse than tastes
in monasteries or meeting places.
The domesticated Wind-deer
was brought under Victor’s sway by tastes.
Accept the Ass: a past life story (Ja 15 1.1)

“Please accept the eight-hooved ass,
the deer more wily than the wily.”
“He has skipped the appointment seven times—
I’ll make no attempt to instruct him.”
The Triply Collapsed Deer: a past life story (Ja 16 1.1)

“About that deer—triply collapsed with many illusions,
eight-hooved, a midnight drinker—
he’s breathing on the ground through one nostril!
Excelling with these six tricks, he deserves a chance.”
Gales: a past life story (Ja 17 1.1)

Whether the moon is waning or waxing,
it is cool when the gale blows.
Since the wind brings the cool,
both are undefeated in this instance.
The Feast for the Dead: a past life story (Ja 18 1.1)

If beings only knew
how this suffering is created by birth,
no creature would kill another,
for the slayer of creatures grieves.
The Vowed Feast: a past life story (Ja 19 1.1)

If you would be released, after death might you be released,
because releasing binds.
That’s not how the attentive are released;
such release is the fool’s bondage.
The Reed Drink: a past life story (Ja 20 1.1)

Seeing footprints go down into the water,
and none that return,
we shall drink water through a reed:
no way shall you kill me.
The Four-horned Antelope: a past life story (Ja 21 1.1)

The four-horned antelope knows that
it’s you who tosses fruit from the beechwood tree.
I’ll go to another beechwood,
I don’t like your fruit.
Hounds: a past life story (Ja 22 1.1)

The dogs raised in the royal family,
pedigreed, handsome and strong,
are not slaughtered, we are slaughtered—
this is not the mutts deserving death, this is the killing of the weak.
The King’s Thoroughbred: a past life story (Ja 23 1.1)

Though lying on my side
pierced by many arrows,
the king’s stallion beats a gelding—
harness me now, charioteer.
The Thoroughbred: a past life story (Ja 24 1.1)

Whenever whenever, wherever whenever,
wherever wherever, whenever whenever:
the thoroughbred drives onward,
while the geldings fade right there.
Fords: a past life story (Ja 25 1.1)

At one ford or another
lead the horse to drink, rider.
For man who overeats,
even milk-rice is a torment.
The Elephant Named Ladyface: a past life story (Ja 26 1.1)

Before, hearing the speech of the bandits,
Ladyface went on a rampage.
But hearing the speech of the well-restrained,
the supreme elephant is established in all good qualities.
Frequent: a past life story (Ja 27 1.1)

It’s not enough to give him a morsel,
a bite, some grass, or a rubbing-down.
I think by seeing the dog often,
the elephant grew fond of him.
The Ox Named Nandivisāla: a past life story (Ja 28 1.1)

One should only speak sweetly,
never not sweetly.
For the one speaking sweetly,
a large load was pulled,
earning him money,
and he was satisfied with that.
The Ox Named Black: a past life story (Ja 29 1.1)

No matter how heavy the load,
or how deep the passage,
when they harness Black,
he pulls that load.
The Pig Named Munika: a past life story (Ja 30 1.1)

Envy not what is Munika’s,
for he eats the food of the terminally ill.
Don’t worry, just eat your chaff,
this is a mark of long life.
Nests: a past life story (Ja 31 1.1)

Mātali, don’t ram the bird nests
in the red silk-cotton woods with your draft-pole.
I’d rather give up our lives to the titans
than deprive these birds of their nests.
Dancing: a past life story (Ja 32 1.1)

Your cry is sweet, your back brilliant,
your neck the color of sapphire,
and your feathers a full fathom long;
still, because of your dancing, I will not give you my daughter.
Agreement: a past life story (Ja 33 1.1)

In agreement, the birds fly,
taking away the net.
But when they start arguing
they’ll come under my sway.
The Fish: a past life story (Ja 34 1.1)

It’s not the cold or heat for me,
nor the being caught in the net;
it’s that my lady, the fish, thinks of me,
“He went for joy to another.”
The Quail: a past life story (Ja 35 1.1)

I have wings that do not fly!
I have feet that do not walk!
Mother and father have fled!
Jātaveda the fire: go back!
Bird: a past life story (Ja 36 1.1)

You sky-flyers staying near the great evergreen,
this fire is emerging!
Geese! Flee to the quarters!
The threat is born from the refuge!
The Partridge: a past life story (Ja 37 1.1)

Those people who honor the elder
are experts in the teaching;
praised in this life,
they’re destined for happiness in lives to come.
